summary.text: Schrödinger's cat is a thought experiment in which a cat in a sealed box is linked to a random atomic event and so seems to be both alive and dead until someone looks.
Erwin Schrödinger devised it in 1935, in talks with Einstein, to show what he saw as the absurdity of Bohr and Heisenberg's views.
It was never meant to be run on a real cat, but it became a standard way to discuss when superpositions end and how quantum mechanics should be interpreted.

facts.label: Devised by
facts.value: Erwin Schrödinger, in 1935, in a discussion with Einstein

facts.label: The trigger
facts.value: A Geiger counter detects one decaying atom and breaks a poison flask

facts.label: Original purpose
facts.value: A critique, using reductio ad absurdum, of the prevailing view

facts.label: Real experiments
facts.value: Atom-scale objects have been shown in superpositions

facts.label: What it asks
facts.value: How long superpositions last and when they collapse

items.prompt: A friend says Schrödinger built his cat scenario to prove cats really can be both alive and dead. What is the best reply?

options.label: He meant it as proof, and later physicists agreed
He used it to promote the idea of undead cats
He meant it to expose how absurd that view seems
He ran it with real cats in 1935

items.explain: Schrödinger did not want to promote dead-and-live cats as serious; he used reductio ad absurdum against the existing view of quantum mechanics.

items.prompt: What links the cat's fate to the quantum world in the original setup?

options.label: Poison released when a Geiger counter sees a decay
A timer that opens the box once each hour
A camera that watches the cat from outside
A scale that keeps measuring the cat's weight

items.explain: If the monitor detects a single atom decaying, the flask shatters and the poison kills the cat; otherwise the cat lives.

items.prompt: You open the box and find the cat. What do you see, and why is it puzzling?

options.label: A half-alive cat that is hard to picture
One state only, so when did the mix end?
Two cats, one alive and one dead
Always a dead cat, so it is rigged

items.explain: The wave function is a combination of both possibilities, yet looking shows only one, which raises the question of when superposition ends.

items.prompt: Could a laboratory today put a whole cat into a superposition just as it does a single atom?

options.label: Yes, and it is routine
No, since atoms can never be in superpositions
Yes, but only in the dark
Not practically, because large objects pose huge technical difficulties

items.explain: Atomic-scale experiments show very small objects can exist as superpositions, but doing so for something cat-sized would pose considerable technical difficulties.

items.prompt: Einstein suggested a keg of gunpowder as an example. What point did it make?

options.label: Big systems can also end up in a mixed state
Gunpowder is unstable and hard to store
Kegs are too large for quantum theory
Explosions are always fully predictable

items.explain: Einstein pointed out that an unstable keg's state would, after a while, contain a superposition of exploded and unexploded states.

items.prompt: Why do physicists still discuss the cat decades later?

options.label: It proved the Copenhagen view correct
It compares how different interpretations handle the measurement problem
It gives a recipe for building quantum computers
It was the first experiment on large animals

items.explain: The thought experiment remains a touchstone and can be used to compare the strengths and weaknesses of interpretations of quantum mechanics.
